articles.title: Rochdale council deputy leader detained briefly in Pakistan during civic visit
articles.excerpt: Councillor Daalat Ali was held for a short time upon arrival in Pakistan as part of a delegation aimed at strengthening ties with Sahiwal.
articles.content_html:
Councillor Daalat Ali, the deputy leader of Rochdale council, was detained by authorities for a short period upon his arrival in Pakistan. This incident occurred during a civic delegation visit to the city of Sahiwal, which is twinned with Rochdale.

The delegation includes Rochdale's ceremonial mayor, Councillor Faisal Rana, and aims to strengthen relationships between the two areas, which have historical ties dating back to their twinning in 1998.

The council confirmed that the detention was brief and related to Councillor Ali's long-standing personal campaigning regarding the Kashmir region. A spokesperson for the council stated that such detentions are not uncommon for individuals travelling to this region, particularly those with political views.

Councillor Ali is reported to be safe and well, having continued his travels and meetings with local officials after the incident.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office also acknowledged the situation, confirming that they were in contact with local authorities regarding the matter.

While the exact reasons for Councillor Ali's detention have not been officially confirmed by Pakistani authorities, the council's statement reassured that he was able to resume his duties as part of the delegation shortly thereafter.

This visit is significant for Rochdale, as many residents have familial connections to Sahiwal.

The delegation's activities include attending various events, such as the opening of a Sewing Machine Centre by the Al-Mahmood Foundation, which is part of the ongoing efforts to foster community ties and support local initiatives in both regions.

articles.title: Heywood prepares for Remembrance Day services on 8 November 2026
articles.excerpt: The borough of Rochdale will hold Remembrance Day services across various townships, inviting public participation to honour servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
The borough of Rochdale is set to hold Remembrance Day services on Sunday, 8 November 2026, across various townships, including Heywood. The council has extended an invitation to all members of the public to attend these commemorative events, which aim to honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women, both past and present.

In a statement, the Mayor of Rochdale expressed the importance of community solidarity during this time of remembrance. The council is committed to supporting all members of the armed forces community, ensuring that their contributions are recognised and appreciated by the public.

Poppies, a symbol of remembrance, can be purchased at Number One Riverside in Rochdale and other designated locations. They are available for purchase online through the Royal British Legion's website.

The public is encouraged to wear poppies as a mark of respect and gratitude towards those who have served in the armed forces.

As the date approaches, residents are reminded of the significance of Remembrance Day and the opportunity it provides to reflect on the sacrifices made for peace and freedom. The council looks forward to seeing a strong turnout from the community to pay their respects.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debits delayed by one day after system error
articles.excerpt: Council Tax Direct Debits due on Monday 26 October will instead be collected on Tuesday 27 October, Rochdale Council says. The notice applies to the affected collection date.
articles.content_html:
Residents whose Rochdale Council Tax Direct Debit was due to leave their account on Monday 26 October 2026 should expect it to be collected on Tuesday 27 October instead, following a system error at the council.

The authority has placed a notice across its official website explaining that payments scheduled for Monday 26 October will be taken one day later. It has not said in that notice how many accounts are affected, what caused the error or whether any other collection dates will change. The published change concerns this specific Monday collection date, not every Council Tax instalment.

For residents who budget closely around outgoing payments, the practical point is to leave enough money in the account for the revised Tuesday collection. A payment not showing as taken on Monday does not, by itself, mean the instalment has been cancelled. Residents should avoid making an additional manual payment simply because the usual Direct Debit has not yet appeared, without first checking their account or speaking to the council.

The council says residents can check their Council Tax balance through its MyAccount service. People who need help can contact the Council Tax team on 0300 303 8870. These are official council channels; no bank details should be supplied to an unsolicited caller or message claiming to be about the delay.

The notice was checked on Monday 26 October. It does not explain whether customers will receive individual notifications. Rochdale Daily will update this report if the council announces any further change.

Official information: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/counciltax. Council Tax account guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/council-tax-account-balance-enquiries. Council contact details: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/contactcentre.

articles.title: Safeguarding concerns, community costs and fireworks raised at Rochdale council meeting
articles.excerpt: Farooq Ahmed raised concerns about safeguarding powers, while Jordan Tarrant-Short questioned venue costs, fireworks, foster care and Warwick Mill at full council.
articles.content_html:
Concerns about the potential misuse of safeguarding powers, community venue charges and fireworks nuisance were raised during Rochdale’s full council meeting on Thursday, October 15.

Councillor Farooq Ahmed questioned how the council prevented staff from overstepping their authority, while Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short pressed cabinet members on issues including foster-carer recruitment, Warwick Mill and access to community facilities.

Councillors also rejected a proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments and backed motions concerning energy costs in new homes, protecting pubs and condemning attacks on places of worship.

Concern over safeguarding powers

Ahmed stressed that protecting vulnerable adults and children must come first, but questioned whether safeguarding procedures could sometimes harm the people they were intended to protect.

He said some officers could overstep their authority, leaving service users and families feeling victimised. He suggested the term safeguarding could be abused and asked how the council ensured staff did not misuse their powers.

Councillor Shah Wazir said safeguarding should protect and support people without causing avoidable distress. He outlined expectations around involving residents in decisions, providing advocacy where required and reviewing complaints and practice.

Responding to Ahmed’s supplementary question, Wazir invited him to provide specific incidents and promised they would be examined. The mayor also encouraged Ahmed to report his concerns.

The exchange raised concerns about potential misuse; it did not establish that misconduct had occurred in any particular case.

Community groups facing venue costs

Tarrant-Short said community organisations had contacted him about hire charges at facilities managed by Your Trust, warning that costs could make their activities financially unsustainable.

He told the meeting that a local dance group had reported being quoted £11,000 for one evening at Heywood Civic Centre. The booking requirements and an explanation of that reported quotation were not established during the exchange.

He asked whether protections, concessions or community pricing policies could prevent voluntary organisations being priced out.

Councillor Sue Smith said reduced rates or room-hire waivers could be available where appropriate, but charges also had to cover staffing, technical support and other operating costs.

She asked him to send details so officers could investigate. Smith said she had helped groups reduce charges, sometimes through changes to booking dates or times, but did not announce a new borough-wide pricing policy.

Fireworks and stronger safeguards

Tarrant-Short raised residents’ concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year, describing distress to families, vulnerable people and pets.

He asked what action the council and partner agencies were taking, then pressed for lobbying for stronger regulation and enforcement powers.

Councillor Tricia Ayrton acknowledged the concerns and said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response.

She also said the council’s three community bonfire events would use reduced-noise fireworks, accompanied by music and lights. In response to his request for stronger national action, she encouraged councillors to raise concerns with their MPs.

Recruiting and retaining foster carers

Tarrant-Short asked how the council would increase the number of local foster carers and provide enough family placements for vulnerable children.

Councillor Rachel Massey outlined work through the Greater Manchester fostering recruitment hub, alongside specialist fostering, training and support. She identified particular needs for carers supporting teenagers, sibling groups and children with disabilities.

In a supplementary question, Tarrant-Short congratulated the children’s services team before asking what recruitment targets would replace retiring carers and increase overall capacity.

Massey said recruitment strategies and targets existed, while stressing the importance of finding the right home for each child. She did not give a numerical recruitment target in that exchange.

Warwick Mill and local investment

Tarrant-Short asked whether Warwick Mill would be acquired through compulsory purchase.

Council leader Neil Emmott said the council had negotiated an agreement with the owner and that cabinet had approved exercising an option to purchase following due diligence.

Asked why decisive intervention had taken so long, Emmott pointed to private ownership and previous unsuccessful redevelopment proposals, saying the council was now taking action.

Tarrant-Short also called for more community events in Rochdale South, including his Balderstone and Kirkholt ward.

Later, he asked whether a previously discussed highways review meeting had taken place. Scrutiny chair Councillor Tom Besford said no date had yet been arranged and promised to follow it up with him.

Pub protections and council votes

Tarrant-Short formally moved an amendment to the pub-protection motion, which councillors approved unanimously. The amended motion subsequently passed, supporting action over restrictive covenants that can prevent former pubs reopening.

Councillors unanimously supported motions on reducing energy costs in new homes and condemning attacks on places of worship.

A proposal to rescind the council’s climate emergency commitments was defeated.

Rochdale Borough Council has released its Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy for the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29. This document outlines the council's financial plans and priorities over the next three years.

The report details expected revenue and expenditure, aiming to ensure financial stability and effective service delivery within the borough. It is a crucial step in planning for the future amid ongoing economic challenges.

Local residents and stakeholders are encouraged to review the report, which is available on the council's official website. This transparency allows for community engagement and feedback on the proposed financial strategies.

The council will continue to assess its financial position and make adjustments as necessary, with further updates expected in future council meetings.

articles.title: Five years later, a court summons: Rochdale residents report historic Council Tax demands as arrears reach £28.4m
articles.excerpt: Several residents tell Rochdale Daily they have received summonses for old Council Tax bills, including a 2021 account. With arrears reportedly £28.4m, we examine recovery rules, compare council finances, and list free debt help.
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

Several residents have approached Rochdale Daily reporting that they have received court summonses over Council Tax bills from previous years. One account relates to a bill dating back to 2021 — approximately five years ago. These reports are residents' accounts; the paper has not independently examined the full Council Tax and court history for every case.

For households already struggling with essentials, an old demand coupled with court costs can create significant additional pressure. The issue raises questions about whether Rochdale Council has changed its approach to historic arrears, what notices were originally sent, how payments are allocated and what support is offered before enforcement.

ROCHDALE'S £28.4 MILLION COUNCIL TAX ARREARS

Government collection returns for 2025/26, as compiled by Council Tax Helpline, place Rochdale's total Council Tax arrears outstanding at around £28.4 million at 31 March 2026, including recovery-related costs — up approximately 12.7% over the year. This is not the amount owed by any individual and should not be divided among residents as if everybody owes it.

Rochdale Council's draft 2025/26 accounts use a different accounting measure. Their Council Tax debtor balance increased from £19.585 million at 31 March 2025 to £21.958 million at 31 March 2026. Those figures should not be added to the £28.4 million or treated as directly interchangeable; they reflect different financial reporting definitions.

Sources: government 2025/26 collection returns https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/collection-rates-for-council-tax-and-non-domestic-rates-in-england-2025-to-2026; authority comparison https://www.counciltaxhelpline.co.uk/research/council-tax-arrears/; council draft accounts, Note 15 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

CAN THE COUNCIL SUMMON SOMEONE FOR A 2021 BILL IN 2026?

Potentially, yes. Regulation 34(3) of the Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992 generally gives a council six years from the date the sum became due to bring proceedings for a liability order. A bill described as relating to 2021 is not automatically outside that period in October 2026; the precise demand and due dates matter.

A previously granted liability order changes the position, because subsequent enforcement is not necessarily subject to the same six-year limit for starting the original proceedings. Anyone disputing liability or the timetable needs their account history, copies of notices, and dates of any earlier court orders.

Source: Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992, Regulation 34 https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/613/regulation/34

WHAT ARE THE COURT COSTS — AND WHAT SHOULD YOU DO?

Rochdale Council's court-hearings guidance says a summons may carry court costs of £101.50 or £102. If the council obtains a liability order, enforcement fees may increase what someone has to pay. A summons is not proof that the amount claimed is accurate: residents can challenge liability or payment records through the proper process.

Residents should NOT ignore a summons. Ask immediately for the annual bill, statutory reminders, itemised transactions and credits, discounts and exemptions, dates notices were sent, and confirmation of whether a liability order already exists. If challenging liability before magistrates, follow the court-hearing telephone attendance instructions on Rochdale Council's website and the summons itself. Financial hardship alone is not normally a defence to liability, but it is a reason to seek an affordable arrangement and specialist debt advice without delay.

Source: Rochdale Council court-hearing guidance https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/problems-paying-council-tax/3; contact Council Tax 0300 303 8870 or council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk

COULD PAYMENTS BE GOING TO DIFFERENT TAX YEARS?

Rochdale Council explains that its software normally allocates a payment matching a current-year instalment to the current year. A payment matching more than one such instalment can also be allocated to the current balance rather than old arrears. Other payments may go to the oldest debt. Residents seeking to pay arrears for a specific year are advised to tell the council explicitly which year's debt the payment is intended to reduce.

That does not establish an error in any resident's case, but it makes a full payment allocation history essential when a debt resurfaces years later.

Source: Rochdale Council, 'How payments are allocated' https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/pay-council-tax

IS THIS A NEW HISTORIC-DEBT CRACKDOWN?

The public records do not prove that. The council was collecting older arrears before 2026. In October 2023 it reported collecting approximately £2.5 million in Council Tax arrears by the end of that August, about £400,000 more than in the comparable prior period.

To establish whether residents are receiving more summonses for old debts now, Rochdale Daily is seeking year-by-year summons figures broken down by the year of original liability, amounts claimed, recovery costs, cancelled summonses and changes in recovery policy. We have not found such a breakdown in publicly accessible reporting.

Source: Council meeting reports, October 2023 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/g6401/Public%20reports%20pack%2018th-Oct-2023%2018.00%20Council.pdf?T=10

AND WHAT ABOUT THE £50 MILLION UPPERBANKS LOANS?

Rochdale Council's draft accounts show £50.309 million in contractual loans owing from council-owned companies associated with the Upperbanks hotel and residential development at 31 March 2026. During 2025/26 the loans accrued approximately £2.020 million in interest and recorded £132,000 in repayments. Their loan arrangements include payment holidays and other contractual conditions.

These are NOT unpaid household taxes and the size of a commercial loan balance does not, by itself, imply it is overdue or in default. Crucially, no evidence has been established connecting Upperbanks lending with the pursuit of old Council Tax bills. The legitimate point of comparison is whether the council makes its debt-management decisions transparent across both areas of public finance.

Source: Rochdale Council draft 2025/26 accounts, loan disclosure https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

FREE HELP IF YOU CANNOT AFFORD YOUR COUNCIL TAX

StepChange Debt Charity: 0800 138 1111, free advice online at https://www.stepchange.org. Advisers can help prioritise Council Tax arrears, assess household finances, work with creditors and consider suitable debt solutions.

National Debtline: 0808 808 4000, https://nationaldebtline.org. Independent help with Council Tax, summonses, liability orders, enforcement agents and budgeting.

Citizens Advice Rochdale: 0808 278 7803. Rochdale advice sessions include Number One Riverside, Smith Street. Check current drop-in and outreach arrangements at https://www.citizensadvicesort.org.uk/offices/rochdale. Support includes benefits, housing, debt and practical assistance.

MoneyHelper: find free regulated debt advice and budgeting guidance at https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/money-troubles/dealing-with-debt/debt-advice-locator.

Rochdale Council Tax team: 0300 303 8870, council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax. Request an itemised statement, challenge inaccurate liability through the prescribed route, discuss affordable payment arrangements and ask about Council Tax Support.

COUNCIL TAX REDUCTIONS AND EMERGENCY SUPPORT

Rochdale residents on low incomes may qualify for Council Tax Support. Single-person discounts, disability-related reductions and statutory exemptions can apply where conditions are met. The council also has a discretionary Council Tax discount policy under Section 13A of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 for certain exceptional circumstances. Ask the Revenues and Benefits team what evidence is required.

Source: Rochdale Council discretionary Council Tax policy, updated March 2026 https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2426/discretionary-council-tax-discount-policy; Council Tax services https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax

Rochdale's Crisis and Resilience Fund supports eligible residents facing financial emergencies, including certain emergency payments, housing assistance and essential items. It does not automatically settle Council Tax arrears, but may relieve pressure on everyday essentials. Cost of Living Services: 01706 923685. Details at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund.

Some people can obtain a 'Breathing Space' debt respite through an authorised debt adviser. Standard Breathing Space can provide up to 60 days' protection from most enforcement action and interest or charges on qualifying debts, subject to eligibility. A separate scheme exists for qualifying mental health crisis treatment. It does not write off debts. Government guidance: https://www.gov.uk/options-for-dealing-with-your-debts/breathing-space.

SIX QUESTIONS FOR ROCHDALE COUNCIL

1. How many summonses issued in 2025 and 2026 related to Council Tax liabilities originating in 2021 or earlier?

2. Has any targeted exercise or policy change been introduced to recover older Council Tax debts, and when?

3. How much has been added to old balances through court and enforcement costs, and how much was actually collected?

4. How many summonses have been withdrawn because of incorrect liability, missing payment credits, defective notices or limitation issues?

5. What safeguards are used where residents disclose disability, serious illness, unemployment or acute financial hardship?

6. How many residents received repayment arrangements, Council Tax Support or exceptional discounts before enforcement progressed?

Rochdale Daily invites Rochdale Borough Council to respond with records and explanations. The paper also invites residents to share experiences of historic summonses confidentially at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. Do not send personal financial reference numbers or identifiable court documents publicly; redact sensitive information before sharing.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Council Tax is a lawful obligation, and the council can pursue valid arrears. Residents are equally entitled to a clear statement of what they owe, when it became payable, which notices were served, how every payment was credited and what help is available if they cannot pay.

Rising arrears are documented. A new campaign of historic summonses, or a connection to Upperbanks, has not yet been demonstrated. Obtaining the age breakdown of court cases is the next test of the accounts residents have brought to Rochdale Daily.

General information only; individual debt cases require prompt, tailored advice and attention to any court deadline.

articles.title: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

Right of reply: Rochdale Borough Council, the named councillors and the Upperbanks companies can send a response, correction or supporting financial evidence to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Bev Craig and Rochdale: will Greater Manchester's new mayor deliver beyond the city centre?
articles.excerpt: A detailed examination of Mayor Bev Craig's council voting record, Rochdale's deprivation and earnings, affordable housing and transport pledges, and the financial risks behind Greater Manchester's investment plans.
articles.content_html:
Bev Craig's election as Mayor of Greater Manchester leaves Rochdale with a familiar question: will economic growth across the city-region translate into better-paid jobs, more affordable housing and better transport in the boroughs outside Manchester city centre?

Craig, the former leader of Manchester City Council, succeeded Andy Burnham after the mayoral election on 30 July 2026. The official result gave her 309,525 first- and second-preference votes, on a Greater Manchester turnout of 25.14%. Turnout in Rochdale was 22.95%, and she received 15,927 first-preference votes in the borough.

Her pledges on housing, public transport, high streets and industrial regeneration speak directly to several of Rochdale's needs. But the financial distinction between projects approved, investment proposed and outcomes delivered is essential.

ROCHDALE'S DEEPER ECONOMIC PROBLEMS

ONS figures reported through Nomis put Rochdale's employment rate for people aged 16–64 at 67.1% in the year to March 2026, against 75.5% across Great Britain. Estimated unemployment was 7.2%, compared with 4.5% nationally, although the ONS warns that survey-based local unemployment estimates have small-sample limitations.

In 2025, around 33.5% of working-age residents held a qualification at RQF Level 4 or above, compared with 48.6% nationally. The median weekly earnings of full-time employees resident in Rochdale were £689.50, against £766.60 in Great Britain.

According to the Government's 2025 English Indices of Deprivation, Rochdale's employment deprivation measure was 20.3%, among the highest of England's local authorities. A neighbourhood identified as Rochdale 010C has repeatedly appeared among the country's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods.

These figures expose the limitations of equating economic development with prosperity for existing residents. A growing regional economy does not automatically lift household earnings if local people cannot reach the jobs, lack relevant qualifications or cannot afford the homes built nearby.

A MAYOR WITHOUT A PARLIAMENTARY VOTING RECORD

Craig has never served as a Member of Parliament. Burnham was previously the MP for Leigh and a Cabinet minister. Tony Lloyd, the interim Greater Manchester mayor before Burnham, was also an MP.

Craig entered Manchester City Council in 2011 and became its leader in December 2021. Her record must therefore be examined through council and combined-authority decisions, rather than voting divisions or questions in the House of Commons. Attributing parliamentary votes to her would be incorrect.

This distinction is not unusual among English regional mayors. West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, North East Mayor Kim McGuinness and South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard had not served as MPs before taking office. The question is what experience of budgets, national negotiations and local delivery each officeholder brings, not whether a Commons career is a qualification for office.

WHAT HER COUNCIL DECISIONS SHOW

While Craig led Manchester City Council, the authority approved a 2026/27 revenue budget exceeding £1 billion and a 4.99% council tax increase, incorporating a 2% adult social care element. The council said this supported existing services, investment in communities, housing and public provision.

At the Greater Manchester Combined Authority meeting on 13 February 2026, the authority endorsed a Band D mayoral general precept of £153.95: £92.20 relating to fire and rescue and £61.75 to other mayoral functions. The decision followed a named unanimous vote. Compared with the previous year, the Band D precept rose £25.

These decisions were collective, and the latter was a proposal originally brought by Burnham, not a unilateral Craig tax policy. Nevertheless, the record is relevant when evaluating promises to reduce household costs and decisions about how services are paid for.

Craig was also a portfolio lead on the Greater Manchester Good Growth Fund and integrated investment pipeline approved in November 2025. The authority reported initial potential investment capacity in excess of £1 billion and approved borrowing of up to £150 million against future retained business rates.

The phrase '£1 billion investment' should not be mistaken for £1 billion in unencumbered grants. Parts of the programme involve repayable finance, borrowing or contributions from other institutions. How much is ultimately invested, and where, is more meaningful than the initial headline figure.

AFFORDABLE HOUSING: WHAT DOES THE PROMISE MEAN FOR ROCHDALE?

Craig has pledged 50,000 council, social and genuinely affordable homes across Greater Manchester by 2039, including 10,000 homes delivered, under construction or in the pipeline by May 2028.

The three categories in that near-term target are not equivalent. A completed home can be occupied. A home under construction may still face delivery risks. A home in the pipeline may lack full financing or planning approval.

Over roughly 13 years, 50,000 homes implies an average of nearly 3,850 annually across the region, although actual delivery is unlikely to be evenly spread. The programme relies on public and private land, delivery partners and capital funding that will vary from scheme to scheme.

Rochdale needs published borough-specific targets, a social-rent breakdown, site-by-site funding and delivery dates. 'Affordable' as a statutory housing designation is not always affordable for a household on below-average wages.

TRANSPORT: AN AREA WHERE THE MAYOR HAS DIRECT SPENDING CHOICES

Burnham's transport legacy includes the Bee Network and bringing local buses under public control. Craig has committed to extending free Bee Network bus travel to young people aged 11–16, building on the existing scheme for those aged 16–18.

Transport for Greater Manchester estimates that nearly 200,000 young people could benefit, saving families up to about £500 per eligible child a year. The proposed start date is January 2027, but detailed eligibility and the formal decision process have yet to be completed. The combined authority's forward plan lists a relevant decision for November 2026.

There is a financial trade-off: cheaper travel can widen access to education and employment, while recurring concessions can create continuing expenditure or foregone fare income. An annual programme budget, estimates of extra journeys and bus capacity would make the policy's cost clearer.

Meanwhile, Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton have longstanding demands for stronger rail and tram links. Early development funding for the Oldham–Rochdale–Heywood–Bury tram-train concept should not be confused with an approved construction budget.

In a September 2026 parliamentary answer to Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell, the Department for Transport confirmed that Greater Manchester is due £2.5 billion in Transport for City Regions funding between 2027/28 and 2031/32, and that scheme prioritisation rests with the mayor. That does not mean all of the money is free for the tram proposal: other regional transport commitments compete for the same settlement.

MIDDLETON AND ATOM VALLEY

Middleton is a practical test of whether investment can extend beyond Manchester's commercial centre.

On 25 September 2026, the GMCA approved the proposed designation of a Middleton mayoral development area, subject to the borough council's consent. Rochdale Council Cabinet endorsed the plans on 29 September. The proposed Middleton Co-operative Mayoral Development Corporation is intended to coordinate land, investment and regeneration.

A development corporation can help assemble and develop sites, but the designation alone creates neither jobs nor homes. Residents will need to know the initial public expenditure, which businesses are being attracted and whether vacant premises are being brought into productive use.

Atom Valley and plans for a Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre offer the possibility of advanced manufacturing employment in Rochdale. Earlier GMCA proposals included an indicative allocation of up to £15 million for the centre. Indicative funding, however, is not evidence that the whole scheme has been built or that local recruitment benefits have been achieved.

Craig's proposed £20 million Good Growth High Streets Fund raises a similar question. Although a simple division across Greater Manchester's ten boroughs would imply £2 million each, that is not the fund's published allocation mechanism. The official forward plan schedules the launch decision for 13 November 2026. Its distribution and final conditions remain important.

IS THE ECONOMIC PROGRAMME FINANCIALLY FEASIBLE?

Three kinds of promise require different financial tests: ongoing services, one-off capital construction and investment meant to generate repayments or returns.

Transport concessions may need continuing annual support. Housing and infrastructure require capital, planning approvals, land and delivery partners. Investment financed by borrowing must produce enough income or wider economic benefit to justify financing costs and risk.

The Good Growth Fund's capacity incorporates future retained business-rates income and borrowing, so its published performance should be judged against debt-service costs, reserves, expected returns and delays. Lower-than-expected project returns could restrict later investment capacity.

There is an economic case for public intervention where contaminated land, weak connectivity or low private returns prevent development. Equally, a funding announcement does not remove the possibility of construction inflation, overruns or weak returns.

None of these observations establishes that Craig's programme is either fully financed or unaffordable. An authoritative judgement requires programme-level budgets that separate committed grants from lending, approved borrowing from available cash, and announced schemes from projects ready to proceed.

HOW OTHER REGIONS ARE APPROACHING THE SAME QUESTIONS

The West Midlands, with a broadly comparable metropolitan scale, has pursued a mix of housing, regeneration and transport investment under Richard Parker. Its announced Futures Fund draws on several funding and investment partners rather than operating simply as a direct grant pot.

In Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram has pursued bus franchising and integrated transport, while South Yorkshire's Oliver Coppard has combined transport reform with access to skills and work. Their regions differ in population, devolved powers, infrastructure and financial structure, making simplistic headline spending comparisons unreliable.

For Greater Manchester, much of the institutional machinery was developed under Burnham: bus franchising, devolved transport decisions, investment coordination and city-region policy-making. Craig inherits that machinery rather than beginning from scratch.

WHAT THE BOROUGH SHOULD BE ABLE TO MEASURE

Rochdale residents should be able to see investment figures broken down by borough and funding type; affordable homes completed and their rents; local recruitment and wages on public-backed schemes; transport projects with approved construction budgets; and the proportion of high-street funding that actually reaches each community.

The same applies to Atom Valley and Middleton. How many genuinely new posts are created? How many go to Rochdale residents? How much public borrowing is involved? Which sites have actually begun construction?

Craig has made commitments that address recognisable challenges in Rochdale. Some draw on programmes already in progress; others remain targets or proposals requiring further approval. The economically meaningful comparison with Burnham and mayors elsewhere will be based on achieved outcomes and published finances, not the number of projects announced.

For Rochdale, the fundamental test is whether city-region investment reaches households facing lower wages, weaker employment prospects and inadequate transport connections — and whether the financial costs of delivering it remain transparent.

articles.title: New Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig visits Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Newly elected Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today as she begins work across the city-region following her victory in last month's mayoral by-election.
articles.content_html:
Newly elected Mayor of Greater Manchester Bev Craig is visiting Rochdale today, bringing the new city-region mayor to the borough during the opening days of her term.

Craig was elected at the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election on 30 July, succeeding Andy Burnham after his return to Westminster. She became the first woman to hold the Greater Manchester mayoralty.

The visit puts Rochdale among the places receiving early attention from the new mayor as she begins the job of representing all ten Greater Manchester boroughs.

At the time of publication, no detailed public itinerary or standalone press release about today's Rochdale visit had been published on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority news pages. Rochdale Daily has checked publicly available material from the mayoral and GMCA press operation and will update this article if further details, photographs or statements are released.

Craig arrives in Rochdale having campaigned on a platform that included expanding the Bee Network, freezing bus fares and extending free bus travel to young people aged 11 to 18. She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

articles.title: Comment: Government changes to local planning risk shutting residents out
articles.excerpt: From October 2026, most planning applications will be decided by officers with no route to a public committee hearing. Castleton councillor David Jones argues the reforms trade local democracy for speed.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Councillor David Jones (Reform UK, Castleton), a member of Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee. The views expressed are his own.

As a member of Rochdale Council's Planning Committee, I want to make residents aware of significant changes being introduced by the Labour Government to the way planning applications are decided.

From 31 October 2026, a new national system will divide planning applications into two schedules.

Schedule 1 applications must be decided by planning officers, with no option for them to be brought before the Planning Committee. This will include householder applications, minor commercial developments and some residential developments of up to nine homes. Regardless of the level of local concern, these applications will not receive a public decision by elected members.

For Schedule 2 applications, the starting assumption will also be that they are decided by officers. They will only come before the Planning Committee if they meet a test relating to significant local or planning issues, and both a nominated senior planning officer and the chair of the Planning Committee agree that committee consideration is warranted. If they cannot agree, the application will remain with officers.

Perhaps most concerningly, ward councillors will lose the ability to call a planning application before the committee. Councils will also be unable to guarantee committee consideration simply because an application has attracted a large number of objections.

Residents will still be able to submit comments and objections, and relevant planning concerns must still be considered. However, making an objection is not the same as having the application examined and debated publicly by elected councillors.

HMOs are a major concern for many Castleton residents. Where an HMO proposal requires planning permission, residents may submit objections, but neither they nor their ward councillor will be able to guarantee that it receives a public committee hearing. Instead, that decision will rest with a senior officer and the committee chair.

The Government says these changes will provide greater consistency and allow committees to concentrate on the most significant developments.

I understand the need for an efficient planning system, but I do not believe efficiency should come at the expense of local democracy.

A planning application that appears "minor" on paper can have a major impact on the people living beside it. Local circumstances cannot always be understood through a national classification or an officer's written report.

In my view, removing councillors' call-in powers takes away an important democratic safeguard. It weakens the ability of elected representatives to ensure that residents' legitimate concerns are heard and debated publicly.

This is not about councillors ignoring planning law or blocking development without proper grounds. It is about retaining openness, accountability and meaningful local representation in decisions that can permanently affect our neighbourhoods.

I will continue to speak up for Castleton residents and raise my concerns about any change that further distances local people from decisions affecting where they live.

Greater consistency should not mean less democracy, and faster decisions should not mean residents having less of a say.

articles.title: Reform UK councillors explain vote against 74-bed Sparth House care home
articles.excerpt: All three Reform UK members of Rochdale's Planning Committee voted against the revised 74-bed care home at Sparth House, saying concerns over scale, trees and parking had not been resolved.
articles.content_html:
All three Reform UK councillors serving on Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee voted against the proposed 74-bed care home development at Sparth House, Manchester Road, when the application returned to the Committee.

The application had previously been deferred after members raised concerns regarding the scale and massing of the proposed building, its impact on neighbouring residents, the loss of mature trees, parking provision and whether the development represented an appropriate use of the site.

In a statement setting out their reasons, the Reform UK group said that when the revised application returned to Committee, its councillors remained of the view that those concerns had not been adequately addressed. Whilst amendments had been made to the application, the group said it did not believe they sufficiently overcame the fundamental planning issues that had led to the original deferral.

"Let us be absolutely clear," the statement said. "Reform UK fully supports investment in high-quality care facilities. We recognise the growing need for dementia and nursing care across Rochdale Borough, particularly as our population ages. However, supporting better care does not mean supporting every planning application regardless of its merits."

The group said every development must be judged on whether it is appropriate for its location, whether it protects neighbouring residents, whether it provides suitable living conditions for future occupants and whether local infrastructure is capable of supporting it.

In this case, the Reform UK councillors concluded that the proposed four-storey building represented an overdevelopment of a constrained site, arguing that its overall scale, height and massing would create an overbearing presence, harm the character of the surrounding area and adversely affect neighbouring residential amenity.

The councillors also said they were concerned by the environmental impact of the proposal, including the loss of mature trees, together with what they considered to be limited meaningful outdoor space for a development accommodating 74 vulnerable residents.

Parking provision remained another significant concern for the group. With 13 parking spaces proposed for staff, visitors, healthcare professionals and servicing vehicles, the councillors considered there to be a real risk of additional parking pressure on surrounding residential streets.

Whilst not a material planning consideration and ultimately a matter governed by Building Regulations, the group said members also noted concerns raised during the planning process regarding the practical challenges of evacuating a four-storey building occupied by elderly and vulnerable residents, including people living with dementia, in the event of an emergency. Although these matters fall outside the planning system, the councillors said they nevertheless formed part of the wider public concerns expressed during the application process.

The statement also criticised the local MP, Elsie Blundell, who the group said had commented critically on the decision on social media rather than engaging with the planning concerns debated by the Committee. "Planning decisions should be based on planning merits, evidence and policy, not reduced to political point scoring," the group said. Ms Blundell has been invited to respond, and any reply will be added to this article.

The Reform UK councillors said their responsibility as Planning Committee members is not to approve applications simply because they provide a particular type of development, but to consider every application impartially against planning policy, the evidence before them and the impact on both existing and future residents.

"Had this application demonstrated an appropriate scale, adequate infrastructure, sufficient parking, suitable landscaping and a design compatible with its surroundings, Reform UK would have had no hesitation in supporting it," the statement concluded. "Good care homes deserve good planning. Residents deserve developments that are both needed and appropriate. We will continue to stand up for both."

Planning applications refused by the Committee can be appealed by the applicant to the Planning Inspectorate.

articles.title: Reform UK councillors reject proposed allowance increase
articles.excerpt: The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.
articles.content_html:
The Reform UK councillor group on Rochdale Borough Council has formally rejected a proposed increase in councillor allowances, with every group member notifying the council’s governance team that they will not accept any additional payout.

The controversial increase was rubber-stamped by Labour councillors present at the full council meeting on Thursday 16 July, with every single Labour member in attendance voting in favour. In contrast, Reform UK councillors voted unanimously against the motion, while other political groups on the council either abstained or voted against. At a time when local residents continue to face significant cost-of-living pressures and squeezed household budgets, the Reform UK group believes it is entirely wrong to increase politician payouts funded by the taxpayer. Each Reform UK councillor has now individually written to council officers to officially opt out of the increase, ensuring the extra funds remain in the public purse.

Speaking on behalf of the Reform UK group, Group Leader Councillor John Taylor said: "Hard-working families across Rochdale are having to make tough financial decisions every single day. The idea that local politicians should push through an increase in their own allowances—as Labour did at the full council meeting on 16 July—is completely out of touch with reality. We were elected to serve our community, not to line our own pockets. Reform UK voted against this increase in the chamber, and every single member of our group has now formally instructed council governance that we will refuse to take a single extra penny. We urge councillors from other parties to do the right thing and follow our lead." Reform UK remains committed to promoting financial responsibility, cutting waste in local government, and ensuring council resources are spent directly on frontline public services for the people of Rochdale.

articles.title: Rochdale MP Paul Waugh appointed education minister: what his new role means for the borough
articles.excerpt: Paul Waugh remains Rochdale's MP while taking on a second role as a junior education minister. We examine his responsibilities, additional salary and what the appointment could mean locally.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale MP Paul Waugh has joined the Government as a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State in the Department for Education while continuing to represent the constituency in the House of Commons.

The appointment was formally confirmed as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's ministerial changes, with Mr Waugh taking up the post on 22 July 2026. Lucy Powell is the Secretary of State for Education and heads the department in which he will serve.

Mr Waugh now holds two connected public roles. He remains Rochdale's elected Member of Parliament, responsible for representing constituents, handling casework, holding surgeries, speaking on local issues and voting in the Commons. Alongside that work, he is now a junior government minister with responsibilities inside the Department for Education.

There is nothing unusual or constitutionally improper about an MP also serving as a minister. Most ministers in the House of Commons continue to represent their constituencies. His appointment does not create a vacancy, require a by-election or transfer his constituency responsibilities to another MP.

However, the ministerial job will substantially increase his workload. Ministers are expected to attend departmental meetings, study submissions from civil servants, help develop policy, answer parliamentary questions, take legislation through Parliament, meet education organisations and defend government decisions publicly.

That means constituents will reasonably expect reassurance that Rochdale casework and local representation will continue at the same level. Much of an MP's casework is managed by constituency and parliamentary staff, but Mr Waugh remains personally accountable to Rochdale voters and will still be expected to maintain a visible presence in the borough.

His precise policy portfolio has not yet been published by the Department for Education. The official government page currently confirms his rank and appointment but does not list a detailed set of responsibilities. It would therefore be premature to claim that he has direct control of a particular area such as schools, special educational needs, colleges or apprenticeships until the department formally allocates those duties.

As a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, he is one of the department's junior ministers. Such ministers commonly oversee a defined group of policies, represent the department during Commons debates, answer written and oral questions, meet professional bodies and work under the direction of the Education Secretary and more senior ministers.

The Department for Education is responsible for education and children's services in England. Its work includes early years provision, schools, teacher recruitment and retention, the curriculum, children's social care, further education, higher education, apprenticeships and skills.

The appointment could give Rochdale a stronger connection to national education decision-making, although a minister is required to make decisions for the country as a whole rather than favouring their own constituency.

Locally, there are several areas where residents and education providers will watch his work closely. These include special educational needs and disabilities, school funding, teacher recruitment, attendance, college provision, apprenticeships and support for children requiring speech, language and communication services.

Mr Waugh has previously highlighted Rochdale's work on SEND and early speech and language support. In June, after hosting a ministerial visit to the borough, he said his job was to ensure Rochdale received every penny and every bit of support it had earned. His new position places him inside the department responsible for much of that national policy, although ministerial rules may limit how directly he can intervene in individual local funding decisions.

His salary is also expected to increase if he claims the ministerial salary attached to the post. All MPs currently receive a basic annual salary of £98,599. The claimed additional salary for a Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State serving in the Commons is £22,375.

That would produce total gross annual pay of £120,974 before tax, National Insurance and pension deductions. Ministerial salaries are separate from parliamentary expenses, which are intended to cover legitimate costs such as employing staff, running offices and travelling for parliamentary duties rather than providing additional personal income.

The increase is paid because ministerial office carries responsibilities beyond those of an ordinary backbench MP. Ministers are members of the Government and are bound by collective responsibility, meaning they are generally expected to support agreed government policy publicly or resign from office.

That obligation can occasionally create tension between the two roles. As Rochdale's MP, Mr Waugh is expected to raise local concerns and challenge decisions affecting his constituents. As a minister, he must also support the Government's education programme and comply with the Ministerial Code.

Having a minister as the local MP can provide greater access to senior figures and a deeper understanding of how government decisions are made. It does not, however, guarantee preferential funding or special treatment for the constituency. Decisions involving grants, schools and public bodies should continue to follow proper departmental processes.

Mr Waugh said he was "delighted" to be joining the Department for Education. His own website announced the appointment on 23 July, a day after the official government record says he took up the role.

The official announcement confirms that he joined an education team led by Lucy Powell, who became Education Secretary on 20 July. Other ministers in the department include Georgia Gould, Baroness Smith of Malvern and Josh MacAlister.

For Rochdale, the main test will be whether Mr Waugh can manage the demands of government while continuing to respond effectively to residents. Constituents should still contact his office about immigration cases, benefits, housing, public services and other matters requiring assistance from their MP.

His appointment raises Rochdale's profile within Westminster and places its MP closer to decisions affecting schools, children and skills across England. The title alone will not determine whether the borough benefits. That will depend on the responsibilities he is eventually given, the policies he helps deliver and whether residents continue to receive effective representation from their MP.

articles.title: Heywood MP congratulates Bev Craig and calls for stronger investment in the north of the borough
articles.excerpt: Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on becoming Mayor of Greater Manchester, with both Labour politicians expected to work together on transport, regeneration and investment priorities across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Heywood and Middleton North MP Elsie Blundell has congratulated Bev Craig on her election as Mayor of Greater Manchester, pledging to work closely with the new mayor to secure investment, improve transport and strengthen opportunities for communities across the constituency.

In a public letter following the mayoral election, Blundell said voters had 'reaffirmed their belief that only Labour can deliver on hopes for a fairer Greater Manchester that works for everyone'. She added that she looked forward to working with the new mayor to grow the economic and cultural future of towns including Bamford, Castleton, Heywood, Middleton, Norden and Spotland.

The MP said her priorities remain focused on creating 'a positive future' for both towns and their residents, supporting jobs, culture and regeneration while responding to the wishes of local communities.

Transport featured heavily in her message. Blundell described the current journey from Heywood into central Manchester by public transport as 'unacceptable', saying many young professionals and families need a quicker and more reliable connection to the city. She reiterated her support for extending Metrolink to Heywood, noting that previous commitments had suggested 'spades in the ground' by 2028, and called for continued confidence in delivering the project.

She also welcomed the success of the Bee Network but stressed that towns outside Manchester city centre must not be left behind. Buses and future tram connections, she argued, both have an important role to play in improving connectivity across the constituency.

Blundell highlighted the opportunities presented by the Mayoral Development Corporations planned for Middleton and Atom Valley, describing them as exciting regeneration projects that could combine investment with skills development for both young and older residents. She said it was essential that local people were first in line to benefit from the jobs and opportunities created by future investment.

For residents across Heywood and the wider Rochdale borough, the relationship between the new Mayor and the local Labour MP could prove significant. With both politicians representing the same party, supporters argue there may be greater scope for joined-up working between Westminster, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and local councils when bidding for funding, infrastructure projects and devolved investment.

Whether that political alignment ultimately translates into tangible improvements remains to be seen, but transport projects, regeneration schemes and skills investment are all areas where cooperation between regional and national politicians can help unlock funding and accelerate decision-making.

The timing is particularly important for Rochdale Borough Council. The authority has previously warned of significant long-term financial pressures, with forecasts indicating a funding gap that could reach around £16 million by the end of the decade if additional savings or funding are not identified. While the Mayor of Greater Manchester does not directly control council finances, the Combined Authority plays an increasingly important role in distributing regeneration funding, transport investment, housing programmes, brownfield development grants and skills funding across the city-region.

That means a strong working relationship between the Mayor, local MPs and council leaders could improve the borough's chances of securing external investment for projects that might otherwise place further pressure on local budgets. Investment in transport infrastructure, town-centre regeneration and employment initiatives can help stimulate economic growth, attract private investment and broaden the local tax base over time.

However, the partnership alone cannot solve every financial challenge. Local government funding remains largely determined by central government, while council tax income, business rates and rising demand for statutory services continue to place significant pressure on council budgets across England.

Ultimately, constituents will judge the success of the new political partnership not by the warm words exchanged after the election, but by whether it delivers visible improvements. Faster public transport, investment in Heywood and Middleton, better roads, stronger town centres, more employment opportunities and increased funding for local services are among the outcomes residents will hope to see over the coming years.

With both Elsie Blundell and Bev Craig committed to Labour's vision for Greater Manchester, attention now turns from congratulations to delivery. The coming mayoral term will determine whether that political alignment results in lasting benefits for communities across Heywood, Middleton and the wider Rochdale borough.
